source.title: ChromaFormer: A Scalable and Accurate Transformer Architecture for Land Cover Classification
source.authors: Ming-Shi Li; D. Grujicic; Ben Somers; Stien Heremans; S. De Saeger; Matthew B. Blaschko

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling laws as motivation and studies model scaling for multispectral image segmentation, but does not test the specified language-model loss laws or fit power laws to its results.
record.gate_note: The study reports image-segmentation accuracy and scaling coefficients, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy. It does not fit or assess power-law curves. Rows record its parameter-scale accuracy results and selected training-data-fraction results; these do not measure a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: A method paper proposing ChromaFormer for multispectral land-cover segmentation. It cites Kaplan et al. as motivation and reports overall accuracy and a custom scaling-efficiency coefficient across model sizes and training-data fractions. It fits no power law and reports no held-out loss, compute-optimal split or extrapolation, so its results cannot show whether any version's power-law form holds. The 'scaling' results compare the authors' own architecture against baselines.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that larger models with suitable architectures (ChromaFormer, Swin) clearly outperform UNet++ and ResNet on the large BVM dataset, and that model complexity should be matched to dataset scale. They note two limits: results come from one region, and hardware constraints prevented scaling ChromaFormer further.
record.recipe_differences: Multispectral image segmentation on the BVM dataset; evaluates overall accuracy and a custom scaling-efficiency coefficient, rather than language-model pretraining cross-entropy or power-law fits.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported accuracy varies with architecture, parameter size, and training-data percentage. The text also describes different training-loss curve behavior across model families and training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: BVM segmentation accuracy rises with parameter count within each family, with diminishing returns. ResNet goes from 75.9% at 1M to 89.2% at 2800M. Swin and ChromaFormer models of 27M already reach about 91–92%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In large-scale multispectral segmentation, accuracy gains from model size depend strongly on architecture family; no power-law form is assessed.

fits_no_version.finding: With 5% of training data, accuracy is about 58–66% for all sizes. At 50%, larger transformer models pull ahead (about 91% vs about 74% for small ResNets).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of larger models grows with training-set size in this segmentation setting.

record.problems: Experiments use only the BVM dataset from the Flemish region. The authors report hardware constraints limited further model scaling. The study reports accuracy and custom scaling coefficients rather than fitting power laws; the loss curves are described qualitatively.
record.rows_left_out: Table IV results at 10%, 30%, and 100% training data are omitted to stay within the row limit; the omitted entries are in Table IV. Figure 7's qualitative loss-curve descriptions are not tabulated as rows because they are not held-out pretraining cross-entropy results.

untested.parts: No language models, held-out pretraining loss, or power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and data.

Architecture families (ResNet vs Swin) differ greatly at similar parameter counts, but this is segmentation accuracy across model families, not language-model loss across depth and width within a family.
Multispectral vision setting, but accuracy versus size and data is reported without any power-law fit. The loss curves (Fig. 7) are training loss, described only qualitatively.
No relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance; no language-model downstream tasks.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Several rows are the authors' own method (ChromaFormer) compared with baselines; they are correctly left unlinked to any version. The scaling coefficient S is the paper's own efficiency metric, not a power-law exponent. The Fig. 7 loss curves are moving-average training loss and were correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No language models, held-out pretraining loss, or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget optimization or parameter/token allocation.
The study compares architectures using segmentation accuracy, not language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Although the task uses multispectral imagery, the study does not test whether the same power-law form holds: it reports accuracy and a custom scaling coefficient, without fitting power laws.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.
